narrative:
The 2024 Boston Red Sox were a team that never quite found its footing, stumbling out of the gate and spending much of the year treading water in a competitive AL East. From the very first weekend of the season, the bullpen was already hemorrhaging runs, and early series against Baltimore exposed a relief corps that simply couldn't hold late-game leads. The offense, anchored by Rafael Devers and a surprisingly productive Tyler O'Neill acquisition, provided enough moments of brilliance to keep the season from spiraling — but never enough sustained excellence to push Boston into genuine contention.

The summer months told the story of a team caught in perpetual mediocrity. July was an especially brutal month, with Zack Kelly suffering through a string of catastrophic outings and Kenley Jansen proving unreliable in the closer role. A July 4th implosion against Miami, followed by a Freddie Freeman grand slam off Brennan Bernardino, and then consecutive blown leads against Colorado and New York in late July, encapsulated a bullpen that was costing the team as many wins as the offense was providing. The Red Sox were spinning their wheels, and the window for a playoff push was quietly closing.

August offered brief glimpses of hope — Ceddanne Rafaela's home run, Enmanuel Valdez stepping up with a clutch double — but Kenley Jansen continued to be a liability, surrendering two crushing home runs that month alone. Then came September, and Tyler O'Neill delivered the season's single most impactful play: a three-run home run for his 30th of the year that briefly rekindled postseason dreams. Romy Gonzalez added a late three-run shot to keep the pulse going, but it was too little, too late. Aaron Judge's grand slam off Cam Booser in mid-September was a symbolic gut punch, a reminder that the elite teams in the division simply had too much firepower.

In the end, 81-81 was both an honest and a frustrating final line. The Red Sox scored more than enough runs to contend, but a bullpen that ranked among the most damaging in baseball by high-leverage performance erased too many opportunities. Devers was dependable, O'Neill exceeded expectations, and young players like Rafaela and Gonzalez showed promise — but the lack of elite pitching depth meant Boston finished exactly where their run differential suggested they belonged: squarely on the playoff bubble, watching October from home.

chapters.title: Opening Day Disasters
chapters.description: The Red Sox open the season with immediate bullpen failures, surrendering leads in back-to-back series against Seattle and Baltimore.

chapters.title: Devers Keeps the Ship Afloat
chapters.description: Rafael Devers provides back-to-back clutch doubles in April and May, giving Boston a lifeline and keeping them within striking distance.

chapters.title: Summer Unraveling
chapters.description: A brutal stretch from late June through July sees Zack Kelly, Kenley Jansen, and the bullpen implode repeatedly, costing Boston critical games.

chapters.title: Fleeting August Hope
chapters.description: Scattered offensive bright spots from Valdez, Rafaela, and O'Neill offer brief optimism, but Jansen's continued struggles undercut any real momentum.

chapters.title: Too Little, Too Late
chapters.description: Tyler O'Neill's 30th home run and Romy Gonzalez's late heroics briefly stoke playoff dreams, but Judge's grand slam and the final record of 81-81 tell the true story.
